tagline: Turquoise water, emigrant landmarks and an older road through Bancroft
intro: The Oregon Trail–Bear Lake Scenic Byway begins beside Bear Lake’s turquoise water and links it with the springs and emigrant sites of southeastern Idaho. Visit Idaho highlights those natural and historical attractions and gives the drive as 92.8 miles, taking one hour and fifty minutes. The route uses two-lane roads, with passing lanes on U.S. 30 and a short five-to-six-percent grade at Georgetown Summit. Bear Lake straddles the Idaho–Utah border. Farther north, Georgetown occupies a farming area in the Bear River Valley, between the river and mountains to the east.

Oregon Trail travelers knew Montpelier as Clover Creek, while the carbonated springs at Soda Springs became a landmark farther along their journey. Later highway engineering changed this corridor again: rerouting U.S. 30 over Fish Creek Summit shortened the journey between Soda Springs and Lava Hot Springs but bypassed Bancroft. The scenic byway retains the older route through Bancroft on Blazer Highway.

Heading north from Bear Lake, U.S. 89 connects St. Charles, Paris and Montpelier. U.S. 30 continues through Soda Springs toward Alexander, where the byway turns onto Blazer Highway for Bancroft and Lava Hot Springs. The final stretch follows U.S. 30 west toward Interstate 15 at McCammon.

moments.title: Paris
moments.text: Paris’s red sandstone tabernacle was built between 1884 and 1889 in the Romanesque Revival style. Joseph Don Carlos Young designed the church, which seats around 1,400 people. The town that grew here began with Mormon settlers led by Charles C. Rich in 1863. They believed they had settled in Utah until an 1872 survey put Paris in Idaho. U.S. 89 links Paris with Montpelier to the northeast and Logan, Utah, to the southwest. The setting is a high Rocky Mountain valley, with ranching on much of the surrounding land. The tabernacle’s seating capacity exceeds the town’s 2020 population of 541.

moments.title: Montpelier
moments.text: The old Bank of Montpelier retains its original vault inside the building erected in 1891. Five years after that construction, Butch Cassidy, Elzy Lay and Henry “Bub” Meeks robbed the bank on August 13, 1896. They escaped with roughly $7,000. The building now houses the Butch Cassidy Museum. Earlier travelers knew the settlement as Clover Creek, then Belmont; Brigham Young named it Montpelier after Vermont’s capital. A plaque on Washington Street commemorates the robbery. The National Oregon-California Trail Center stands on the Clover Creek Encampment site, connecting the town’s earlier name with the emigrant route that passed here.

moments.title: Soda Springs
moments.text: A search for hot water produced Soda Springs’ cold-water geyser. In 1937, drilling for a bathing pool struck pressurized carbon dioxide and cold water. The resulting eruption ran for weeks and flooded downtown before the geyser was capped. Releases initially happened by request; a timed valve later put the eruptions on an hourly schedule. The city’s hundreds of carbonated springs had already made it an Oregon Trail landmark in the nineteenth century. The geyser erupts from a travertine mound with viewing platforms at either end. Interpretive signs on the platforms explain how the geyser works, beside the travertine mound where it erupts.
